articles.title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Racial and ethnic minority patients receive less pain treatment than non-Hispanic White patients, and large language models (LLMs) used as medical AI could reproduce that bias. Prior audits tested a few proprietary models, stated race explicitly and rarely measured the models' own response instability. In exploratory, non-preregistered analyses, Study 1 had four open-weight LLMs assess six acute-pain vignettes in every combination of four races and two sexes, with identity stated or cued only by a name (two names per group), comparing each identity with a White male reference on the same case and sampling seed. In Study 2, 24 configurations of 17 models, including OpenAI's GPT-4.1 mini and gpt-oss, Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, Meta's Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, with reasoning on and off and at two precisions, answered the same vignettes and the 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases. In this single-prompt, JSON-constrained task, no difference survived correction in Study 1, none of 1,386 comparisons survived the false discovery rate in Study 2, and every pain-severity difference was equivalent to zero within one point on a 0-10 scale (within a quarter point for 237 of 238 Q-Pain comparisons). Opioid decisions were bounded less precisely (Study 1 could not exclude differences of about 20 percentage points), so they show no detected difference, not proof of none. The few differences surviving correction within a model favoured Black patients. Models differed far more from one another and across their own settings than between patients (the reference patient received the high opioid dose in 6% to 93% of responses), although serving software, provider and prompt format also differed. Fairness audits of clinical AI should use several names per group, pair comparisons on the seed, report the noise floor and test each deployed configuration.

articles.title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14748v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.

articles.title: CAFIN: CUDA-accelerated Adaptive Fisher Information Matrix Network Optimization via GPU-Native Kernel Fusion
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Second-order optimizers improve deep neural network training using curvature information, but their practical efficiency is limited by GPU execution overhead. AdaFisher reduces Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) approximation costs through diagonal Kronecker structures and exponential moving averages, yet its PyTorch implementation requires sequential CUDA kernel launches, intermediate tensor allocations, and repeated memory accesses. We introduce CAFIN, a GPU-native CUDA kernel fusion framework that improves AdaFisher execution efficiency without changing its optimization formulation. The proposed approach progressively integrates FIM preconditioner construction, exponential moving average updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum accumulation, weight decay, and parameter updates into fused CUDA kernels. Shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations further reduce memory traffic and intermediate allocations. Experiments using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti and RTX 3060 Laptop GPUs demonstrate up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1-26.9% lower optimizer-step latency. The implementation also eliminates approximately 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU memory allocations per optimizer step. Numerical validation confirms consistency within the predefined FP32 tolerance, while convergence accuracy remains comparable across evaluated datasets and random seeds. These findings demonstrate that CUDA kernel fusion can substantially accelerate second-order optimization while preserving AdaFisher's underlying mathematical formulation and learning behavior.

articles.title: KernelMosaic: An Open Dataset and Agentic Framework for CUDA Kernel Generation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14604v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training large language models to generate efficient CUDA kernels requires supervision spanning diverse computational requirements and iterative code optimization. Constructing this supervision is challenging because of heterogeneous specifications, and useful implementations emerge through iterative complicated testing and refinement. We introduce KernelMosaic, an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories. Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection curate tasks expressed as natural-language descriptions, reference programs, mathematical specifications, and their intersections. To build the solutions and trajectories, our agentic framework guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair, and performance optimization with reusable CUDA guidance and execution feedback. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on KernelMosaic raises correctness from 4%, 0%, and 0% to 88%, 82%, and 16% on KernelBench L1, L2, and L3, respectively, while increasing the fraction of tasks with kernels faster than PyTorch eager at every level. Further training experiments show that supervision from the curated trajectories substantially outperforms direct responses and promotes sustained testing and revision. These results demonstrate that KernelMosaic enables a general-purpose model to achieve substantial gains in CUDA kernel generation.

articles.title: Thompson Sampling using Prior-fitted Diffusion Transformers
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14656v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Thompson sampling is natural randomized strategy for optimizing unknown functions in a black-box manner. In continuous global optimization, Thompson sampling has largely been restricted to Gaussian process priors, as these are essentially the only class for which computing the posterior distribution has been tractable in practice. In this work, we introduce \emph{prior-fitted diffusion transformers}, which are diffusion models that perform Thompson sampling in-context at inference time, after being pre-trained using the prior-fitted network paradigm. To apply these models, we develop a set of practical non-Gaussian priors for general black-box functions---including those that have characteristics that cannot be achieved under Gaussianity, such as priors over unimodal functions. We also quantify the tradeoff between model size and the number of pre-training iterations, and show that these models follow scaling laws akin to those observed in transformers defined over other modalities. Across a set of global optimization benchmarks, we show that prior-fitted diffusion transformers with non-Gaussian priors can achieve improved performance compared to traditional pipelines built on Gaussian processes.
articles.whyItMatters: Influences training cost, quality, and adaptation strategy.

articles.title: Sophon: A Procedural Diagnostic for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score 85-94% on spatial benchmarks (BLINK Spatial, What's Up CLEVR) yet collapse to chance on simple geometric questions when object, scene, and texture priors are stripped away. We introduce and open-source Sophon, a procedurally generated diagnostic of paired colored point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems (1D linear, 2D Cartesian, 2D polar) and four question types (binary, categorical, comparative, quantitative). Across four open architectures (LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL, Idefics3), accuracy clusters at 47-52% while frontier models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) clear 77-83% and humans reach 84-94%. We use linear probes and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to trace the open-weight failures. Probes of the vision encoder (ViT) and language decoder (LLM) recover Sophon spatial information at 83-85% and 80-86% accuracy, respectively, and the language tower's reasoning circuit answers text-only controls (point clouds as sets of coordinates) at +40 pp over visual stimuli. Language tower per-layer attention attribution localizes visual integration to mid-stack layers. At readout, models elevate the correct answer-set tokens but select among them randomly. We localize the mechanism by tuning individual and grouped components across every architecture's stack, including the vision tower (ViT workspace and reader), the projector, and the language tower (LLM workspace and reader). These experiments demonstrate that this mid-stack workspace holds circuitry capable of organizing the spatial signal so that the frozen reader can decode it. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts that circuitry such that 7B-class VLMs answer Sophon spatial reasoning questions at frontier aggregate accuracy. This work suggests that these models do not have a capability gap for spatial reasoning but suffer from a routing bottleneck that targeted fine-tuning repairs.

articles.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

articles.title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14765v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings shows that the benchmarks separate data contexts and model tiers. Auditing candidate queries against causal provenance in the simulation log verifies gold programs without manual annotation, including on multi-event composite tasks that expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents. We hope the community uses SynthCorp to generate more challenging and useful data estates and benchmarks that foster the development of enterprise data agents.
articles.whyItMatters: Relevant to deployment, monitoring, and evaluation workflows.

articles.title: An LLM Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. We show that a frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM can instead be adapted into a word-level full-duplex system with little data. Our system is a thinker-talker cascade on an 80 ms frame clock. The thinker keeps the LLM frozen and trains only lightweight adapters and a few new token embeddings (97M parameters); at every frame it emits one token of agent text, with pauses, yields, and onsets represented as tokens of the same vocabulary and kept legal by a finite-state machine. A four-stage curriculum, each stage anchored to the model's own behavior under the previous format, performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours. The talker reads only the thinker's discrete tokens, so the two halves are trained independently. On Full-Duplex-Bench and InteractionBench, the system is competitive with open-source full-duplex systems built through large-scale speech training: among them, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses, backchannels most often, and leads in spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and coherence over long conversations.

articles.title: CoLFA: Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Failure attribution in multi-agent systems requires tracing error formation to identify the decisive error step and the responsible agent. However, agents' division of work and information exchange lead to Interleaved Steps and Cluttered Content, requiring models to link executions and check details in lengthy records. This makes it difficult to balance localization accuracy and token cost. We find that multi-agent collaboration also leaves records of how executions connect and content passes between them as results are formed, providing evidence for tracing error formation. Based on this observation, we propose CoLFA (Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution), which uses collaboration cues to organize the attribution input according to how results are formed, determining which steps are examined and how their content is presented. Through Handoff-Guided Step Expansion and Cross-Referenced Content Organization, CoLFA helps the model focus on examining error formation and the role of each decision while reducing the processing of irrelevant and repeated records. Across five settings spanning Who&When and LongRCA and three backbone models, CoLFA achieves the highest exact step-localization accuracy with the lowest token consumption. Compared with individual baselines in each setting, CoLFA improves accuracy by up to 37.50% and reduces token consumption by up to 97.6%.

articles.title: What Entropy-Based View Selection Cannot See: An Audit of Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP can classify images into categories they were never explicitly trained to recognize, but accuracy degrades when test images differ in style or source from their training data. A common remedy generates randomly cropped and flipped copies of each test image, called views, and combines their predictions. Since some views miss the object, methods must identify which views to trust. The dominant approach uses prediction entropy to measure confidence and retains the most certain views. Other methods use signals such as embedding typicality. Despite repeated refinements of these scoring functions, the information they rely on, the model's own response to each view, remains largely unexamined. We investigate this choice while holding other pipeline stages fixed. First, we show that view selection, rather than the gradient update, accounts for almost all accuracy gains. We then examine whether entropy identifies useful views when predictions are wrong, despite at least one view predicting the correct class. In these cases, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones no better than chance, recovering only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views. This finding holds across two image encoders and under a control ruling out an obvious statistical artifact. An exact analysis explains this limitation: entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors. We identify an unused signal already available in the augmentation pipeline: the fraction of the original image retained by each crop. Ranking views by this quantity improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested. A pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.

articles.title: From Classification to Generation: Vision-Language Models for Roman Imperial Coin Description
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cataloguing a Roman Imperial coin involves reading its legends and identifying its imagery in order to match it to an entry in the standard reference catalogue. Previous work has automated individual parts of this process, such as identifying the issuer or recognizing reverse motifs, by formulating each part as a classification task over a predefined set of labels. We instead formulate coin description as image-to-text generation and adapt an open-weight vision-language model (VLM), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, to four tasks: transcribing the obverse and reverse legends, and describing the obverse and reverse imagery. To obtain training data, we convert approximately 30,000 auction records into structured image-text pairs. We separate the two sides of each coin, extract and normalize legends and descriptions, and standardize obverse descriptions against a bust-type taxonomy. We then train a separate low-rank adapter for each task on a single 20GB GPU, and evaluate each task with metrics that we define to capture the key components of numismatic descriptions. The adapted models outperform both the unadapted base model and GPT-4.1 on all four tasks, reducing the normalized edit distance of legend transcriptions by over 40% relative to GPT-4.1. The improvement is smaller, but still present, on legends absent from the training data.

articles.title: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14781v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $\theta$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_\theta$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_\theta$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_\theta$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_\theta$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.

articles.title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14846v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

articles.title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. The code for this paper is at https://github.com/rajesh-lab/code-as-explanations.

articles.title: Graph Label Alignment: A Diagnostic Atlas for Graph Classification
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14760v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph classification benchmarks vary widely in difficulty: some are solved by simple pooled baselines, while others remain challenging for GNNs and graph transformers. We take a data-centric view and ask whether benchmark success is driven by genuine structure--feature reasoning or by label signal already accessible from restricted marginal views. We introduce graph label alignment, a lightweight diagnostic that measures label accessibility through two supervised probes computed without training a graph encoder: structural label alignment (SLA), based on permutation-invariant topological and spectral summaries, and feature label alignment (FLA), based on pooled node features with edges removed. Across real graph classification benchmarks and multiple pooled backbones, the resulting SLA--FLA plane strongly organizes test accuracy, with low-alignment datasets forming a consistent regime where standard pooled pipelines struggle. To probe what lies beyond marginal accessibility, we introduce controlled interaction-dominated stress tests, including heterophilic ego-graphs and synthetic Twins tasks whose structural and feature marginals are matched across classes but whose role--feature couplings differ. These results show that high alignment explains much of easy benchmark performance, while low alignment reveals regimes where success requires preserving structure--feature correspondence beyond standard pooled representations.

articles.title: Benchmarking Multilingual Document Understanding in Vision-Language Models
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. We introduce MDU, a multilingual DU benchmark of 23146 examples spanning 13 tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The tasks isolate complementary capabilities, from surface-level text and Markdown extraction through summarization, classification and named-entity recognition to layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. We evaluate 45 state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system under the same protocol. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average is 69.0, only eight of the 45 evaluated systems reach 65, and the two best results come from 27B models rather than from the largest systems we evaluate. Performance is uneven in ways that scale does not fix. The gap between the strongest and weakest language does not close as models grow, and it survives controlling for the domain composition of each language. Capabilities also do not improve together: once we partial out overall model quality, per-task scores are largely uncorrelated, and transcription ability in particular trades off against semantic extraction.

articles.title: ToolTurns: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Multi-Turn Dialogue
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language models are increasingly deployed in conversational settings, yet most large-scale tool-use benchmarks focus on isolated requests. We introduce ToolTurns, a benchmark of 2,620 problems spanning 1,827 tools and 11,004 API endpoints across 47 categories. Each dialogue begins with an intentionally underspecified request and continues through two context-dependent follow-ups, testing clarification, tool use, and retention of conversational context. We also introduce an open-source user simulator that reveals withheld context through dialogue and generates follow-up requests, with a checker--fixer pipeline for improving its turns. Across nine language models, the best agent resolves 69.6% of individual requests but completes only 39.8% of full dialogues. Under this evaluation protocol, every evaluated model receives lower success scores on follow-up requests than on the initial request, and dialogue-quality rubric scores and task success can rank models very differently. Paired turn-level evaluation shows that the checker--fixer reduces detected dialogue defects, and blind human evaluation favors the revised turns. ToolTurns provides a testbed for evaluating whether agents sustain task success across multi-turn dialogue with tools.
articles.whyItMatters: Directly affects how LLM-powered products are built and shipped.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is out. What did China want from him?
articles.summary: Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode. Huang just resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia as news of his affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, threatened to engulf the company. We’ll have more on that story as things develop and we learn how Nvidia will restructure itself after Jensen — he had something like 60 direct reports, after all, and the entire AI financial ecosystem flows through the company. This is pure Decoder bait. But just two days ago I talked to Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, about the real heart of the scandal: What would China even seek to accomplish by having a spy so close to Jensen? And what does the real state of the US-China AI conflict really looks like, particularly from the Chinese point of view? Kyle’s answers about chips and how China is perceiving the so-called AI “race” were very illuminating, but maybe even more interesting was his observation on Jensen Huang’s relationship with Trump was the most important thing of all — because maybe what China most stood to gain was someone who could whisper in the right ears. Let’s just dive right into it. But keep in mind that when we were talking, we still didn’t know what would happen with Jensen. Okay: Kyle Chan on Nvidia, China, and the future of AI export controls. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Kyle Chan, you are a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. Welcome to Decoder. Great to be here. What on earth could we be talking about as it relates to your expertise about China today? I have a lot to ask you about Nvidia, about our relationship to China as a country, as an economy, and about national security. Let’s start at the very beginning. From all the reporting we have today, it seems like the United States government has been very worried about a company called Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy at the center of the swirling scandal around Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. What do we know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed? We have to be careful about what we know and what we don’t know. So far, there are allegations that the US intelligence community believes that Alice Huang may be an asset of the Chinese intelligence services. Megaspeed itself is a customer of Nvidia’s and they built a data center in Malaysia. They also seem to potentially have ties with Chinese companies and could — and this is where we’re getting into what we do know and what we don’t know — potentially be a conduit for Chinese AI companies accessing cutting-edge Nvidia chips like Blackwells. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. I want to rewind way back. The notion that the Chinese AI industry wants Nvidia chips has been floating around for years and the idea that the Chinese AI industry would somehow develop a parallel set of technology or a superior set of technology because of the constraint of not having Nvidia chips has percolated into the discourse several times. I’m particularly thinking about DeepSeek. DeepSeek launched R1 and it outperformed our models in some ways. We think they didn’t have access to the chips. There are some accusations that they had access to the chips. It turns out they did a bunch of fine-tuning on the chips they did have. What is that relationship like? Do they need the highest-end Nvidia chips? Is it true that they’re actually developing parallel technologies that might be superior to the chips they can have? Just set that stage. A lot of the details are murky, and they’re probably murky for a reason. But up until now, we saw Chinese AI companies that were very heavily dependent on Nvidia chips in order to train and run their models. In fact, they became some of the biggest contributors to the CUDA ecosystem, which is Nvidia’s software ecosystem and platform. They got very good at that, but at the same time with US export controls and greater technology restrictions on access to cutting-edge GPUs, China increasingly pushed these AI companies to switch away from Nvidia to Huawei and other domestic AI chip makers. The idea there is to develop a parallel domestic AI chip supply chain that is good enough, if not on par with, Nvidia’s latest chips, and — crucially — resilient to policy actions coming out of Washington. So that is the story up until this point. The question is, now, what is that trajectory for the Chinese GPU or AI chip development? The reason I wanted to start there is that the motivations to get close to Jensen Huang are very murky to me. As the CEO of Nvidia, I understand that everyone thinks he’s the character and he’s actually in the software designing the next generation of Nvidia GPUs, but he’s just traveling the world giving policy speeches. If you want to build a parallel GPU ecosystem, you’re trying to get close to the designers and the engineers, right? What would be the goal of trying to get close to Jensen Huang? If you wanted the design specs for the latest Nvidia GPUs, I don’t know if you would ask Jensen directly. I think you might want to go to his technical staff. He does have like 60 direct reports. Decoder is often a show about org charts and that one has been on top of my list for a long time, but we’ll set that aside for now. Keep going. What it’s really about is potentially two things. One is trying to understand, maybe to glean information about, the US policymaking process. Jensen Huang is very close to Trump. They talk a lot. Trump can apparently just call Jensen on his cell phone at any moment. In the middle of a conference. We’ve seen the video. On the other side, and maybe this is even the bigger issue, perhaps it’s the biggest concern of all, is the concern that the direction of movement could run the other way, which is that somehow through Jensen, China might be able to influence US policymaking, especially on export controls. That is the big worry from a lot of people in Washington. One of the other underlying concerns here, that I’m just trying to parse out, is that Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, is an executive at a company called Megaspeed. And through Megaspeed, Nvidia may have already been circumventing export controls. It seems like if you’re already solving the problem, maybe you should just leave it alone. How does that dynamic play out? A lot of the story is strange. Even seen in the most cynical terms, it doesn’t quite add up. There could be several different possibilities. One is that this is actually not some concerted strategy from Beijing to try to obtain chips or information or influence, but this is potentially Beijing not quite understanding the full situation and wanting to co-op this Alice Huang person and at least try to understand from her standpoint what is happening. Because I think you’re right. Already you have a very strong relationship between Nvidia and Megaspeed. You also already have — and this is on the influence side — Jensen Huang advocating for his own commercial interests, for a loosening of export controls on his own chips to China. You don’t really need Beijing to push on that gas pedal. That’s already happening. So there are some things that don’t quite make sense if you’re thinking about it from those standpoints, but if you’re thinking about it from the viewpoint of “Beijing wants visibility,” then perhaps that is another plausible explanation. Beijing just wants someone who Trump calls on the phone to advocate for their viewpoints. I see all of that, but what are we getting out of it? If the goal is Nvidia chips, it feels like that is already assured. If the goal is Nvidia engineering plans, that feels like a question mark. If the goal is influence over the Trump administration, I feel like they could have just bought cryptocurrency. [Laughs] That’s right. There’s a big swirl of what is actually happening here. Maybe your point that Beijing just needed more visibility because it is a swirl is the motivating factor. The question that leads me to is that the New York Times reports that US intelligence agencies first flagged these issues a year ago to the Trump administration. There was a memo from Marco Rubio. The reporting is that he oversaw the memo, which is as much plausible deniability as anything. He oversaw it. He was aware that there was a memo. A year ago, the United States’ national security apparatus was worried about Alice Huang at Megaspeed, her relationship with Jensen, and nothing occurred. What do you make of that? That is one of the most worrying aspects of all this. Regardless of what the details are and what is known publicly versus what our intelligence community knows, this is something that should be investigated. This is obviously a major national security issue and this is something where you don’t want someone meddling with this process. You want to do a full investigation, get to the bottom of what’s happening. I think what we’re seeing from some of the reporting is that this has been known, and in fact, if anything, there may have been efforts to try to stop this investigation or distort it in some way. That is very troubling from that internal, within-the-US-government perspective. There’s a lot going on with Nvidia in that part of the story, where Nvidia’s own spokespeople are saying, “There’s nothing going on here. This is a normal relationship,” on the record to many publications. A week later, Jensen issues his apology letter saying there was a relationship. That’s not great for John Rizzo, Nvidia’s comms person. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, is out there saying everything is above board. Now we know not everything is above board. What do you make of Nvidia’s corporate governance here? Because there’s a whole bunch of shareholder lawsuits to come. There’s one filed as of today. I can only imagine there are more to come. Nvidia has to tread very carefully here because what you don’t want is exactly what’s already happening, which is to start to deny or dismiss some of these issues and then turn around and have to say, “Actually, there might be something there.” This is especially important now as there are growing calls for a congressional investigation. So this is going to be separate, perhaps, from within the executive branch where, again, I think we have reasons to worry about conflicts of interest and people not wanting to do this all the way. But if there’s a full-blown congressional investigation, that might reveal some things that, if you are Nvidia, you want to get out in front of rather than have to backpedal later on and explain yourself. Part of the back and forth here with the government’s concern about Alice Huang and Megaspeed is that the Commerce Department spent months looking at the company and then Teter, the general counsel of Nvidia, emailed them and invoked a direct relationship with the Commerce undersecretary, Jeff Kessler. That got the case kicked to the DOJ where everything stopped. Trump yesterday said the FBI is investigating — that’s obviously connected to the DOJ. There’s a universe where the Trump administration is trying to make this go away. Nvidia can pressure the Trump administration to make this go away. That reeks of corruption, obviously. And then you have a very empowered class of Democrats coming into Congress with polling that suggested corruption was one of the top issues in this last election. I don’t see any outcome except those Democrats and an empowered bunch of investigators and an empowered bunch of committee chairs coming after Nvidia as hard as they can. How should the company think about that? Should they just fire Jensen now to get away from it? Should they put them in front of Congress every day for the next year? How do you think that’s going to play out? I think, at the most fundamental level, they need to cooperate and comply with calls from Congress to carry out this full investigation. Because up until now, this has all been so murky, and part of the reason why this has been a stop-and-go, even though those of us in the China AI space have been hearing about this for a while. Companies like Megaspeed, their role in all this, even people like Alice Huang, have been flagged much earlier than this. The fact that this is coming out now, but also that the investigation was stopped and started within the Trump administration, is a big red flag. Ultimately, from Nvidia’s standpoint, they’re going to have to come clean with whatever Congress now requests. There are going to be a lot of hard questions from Congress, as there should be, that have been building up for some time now. If you ever looked at Jensen’s approach to chip export controls, he’s been very fiery that chip export controls are stupid. You mentioned earlier that’s in his business interest. It is better for the Chinese AI industry to be dependent on CUDA and dependent on Nvidia chips, because then if we do get into some conflict, maybe you can restrict that access and you’ll set them back. There’s some swirl of argument that he makes that says it’s in the United States’ national security interest to ship as many Nvidia GPUs to China as you can. Then there are a lot of China hawks who are saying, “Actually, you need to restrain them and keep them years behind. They will not catch up to our bleeding-edge technology. Jensen, you just keep us ahead.” It feels like, out of all of this, the China hawks are going to start winning more fights than they’re losing — arguing that the Chinese government is actively trying to impede our efforts or actively trying to influence our government. How should people think about that? What framework should we use to evaluate that mass of differing opinions, especially now that there’s a catalyst for some kind of change? I think that’s the right way to frame up this whole debate. You have, on the one hand, folks who see the US-China AI competition as a critical strategic competition and access to compute is one of the key levers there, and thus US export controls, not only as they stand now, but tightening them further will be critical to maintaining US edge in the most powerful technology of our lives. Then there are other people who are in the opposite camp who advocate for greater exports of the US AI tech stack writ large, including Nvidia chips and including to China. Up until now, that camp has been led by people like [Commerce Secretary] Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang, and Trump himself. What’s interesting is the balance of power, in terms of whose arguing gets more weight, has been shifting and will shift in light of this recent controversy. So here now those who have been advocating for more exports and fewer export controls, some of their arguments have been tainted by this process potentially, regardless of where the investigation goes. Then there’s a final variable in all this, which is China itself. That’s something that matters a lot in this discussion because in the background, China is doing two things. One, they’re trying to build their own chips and they’re sort of all-in on building a resilient semiconductor supply chain with their own, say, Huawei AI chips that their own AI companies can use. They will never really catch up. It looks highly unlikely, but they could develop good enough chips to replace the Nvidia ones that they have been dependent on for so long. The second big factor from China is retaliation. And this is one thing that I’m watching very closely. If these greater export controls are placed by the US on not just chips to China, but also on chip-making equipment — the tools required to make the semiconductors themselves — will China use its own export controls, such as restricting rare earth metals, to hit back? Right. This is in the context of an ongoing trade and tariff war that has rocked the United States’ economy. In many ways, the first thing that Democrats should do when they enter the next Congress is pass a law getting rid of all the Trump tariffs, right? They’re brought into Congress to fix affordability and the tariffs are an affordability problem, and now we’re going to rush into a trade war with China because we might ask the Dutch government to restrict ASML chip making machines. That seems very fraught to say, “We need to enter into an even more heated AI war with China that might result in the Chinese government placing export controls on the goods that you already find unaffordable.” Do you think that there’s the political will to go through this whole exercise, or is it just to punish Nvidia and Jensen Huang? In some ways, this is happening against the backdrop of other issues that are probably more top of mind for both voters and for incoming legislators in the Capitol. Things like cost of living, as you point out, tariffs, and trying to investigate the Trump administration more broadly for corruption and other issues. Somewhere in there is also the debate around data centers and AI itself. So in some ways, I’ll be curious to see how far this goes, the particular Nvidia issue. There is a scenario where a congressional investigation comes and goes, potentially finds no wrongdoing on Jensen Huang’s part, and then this is just folded into the longer debate around export controls. But there’s another world where if there are issues that come up, that could be potentially disruptive, not just for Nvidia and not just for the US-China relationship, but also for the AI boom in the US overall. Tell me more about China itself. You mentioned that their chips will maybe get good enough. There’s an argument that the models right now, the frontier models we have today, are actually good enough to disrupt the economy. They’re certainly good enough to disrupt the field of mathematics. You could stop training new models and just let the technology diffuse and you would still disrupt huge swaths of the economy today. We’re nowhere close to that actually happening. I think the AI labs should prove that they can do it with the technology they have today. That’s for another time. But China doesn’t need to compete at the frontier to gain the productivity advantages and to gain the industrial advantages. The example I keep using is 5G. I was told for a decade that we had to win the race to 5G, otherwise China would do something and no one would ever tell me what the “something” was. What is the “something” with AI that China will defeat us at that has made this such a critical geopolitical chess match? And is there a point where it will just be good enough for them to achieve that “something”? The funny thing is that China doesn’t see this AI race as being so much about the frontier per se. They’re really much more focused on diffusing the technology. And they think they can “win” the AI race by just having AI used much more broadly and integrated throughout the economy, especially in areas like manufacturing where they are already the behemoth. I think when they see the discussion around getting to AGI, certainly from the government standpoint in Beijing, that to them looks like a bubble and a waste of money. Why are you building all that compute for that? What’s interesting to see is the strategy as they’ve been playing it out is one where they’re trying to not fall too far behind the US, but really focus a lot more on trying to get — especially these open source models — out there across the Chinese economy and globally as well. To that extent, on that metric, they seem to be doing well. That, to me, always has seemed like the real fight. Anthropic and OpenAI are furious that the Chinese companies are constantly distilling their models. They’re trying to build some technology to keep them from distilling their models. But if you believe in the promise of AI and what it can do to the economy, your emphasis should be on diffusing good enough models, not AGI. Whereas our emphasis due to the way our market works is a bunch of guys who think they’re going to build digital Jesus. Whatever is going to happen, that’s the thing they want. [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei has to pretend that he cares about Salesforce, but we know what his real priority is. How do the United States and China compete in that dynamic, where you have one very managed economy that has set a much more near-term and potentially achievable goal, and then our market system where the incentives of the leading market players have nothing to do with the economic incentives of the rest of us? There’s even an ideological foundation to all of this because the vision of AGI is one that is so deeply embedded right now in the American AI community and Silicon Valley culture that I think there’s a risk of potential disconnect, not just between the US and China on this issue, but also within the US, between those who are in the labs like Anthropic and those who are outside who are saying, “Why are we building these giant metal boxes in our backyards? We don’t really see the point of this.” So there’s already that divergence there. Part of it is this longstanding obsession in the American AI imagination with getting to the machine god essentially. Bringing that all back to the context of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, and Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a data center provider in Southeast Asia. It’s theoretically their business. They’re building data centers, they’re buying these chips. Shouldn’t market forces just end this? The United States AI companies want to build data centers. They will pay whatever rates because they have an ideological purpose that is disconnected from capitalism potentially. The Chinese government is just trying to diffuse AI into manufacturing and the United States government would like to hold them back. Shouldn’t market forces just mean that you sell the chips to the highest bidder and the highest bidder will almost always be an American AI company? That’s an interesting question, because there is ultimately market demand in China still for these Nvidia chips. And there’s a divergence here between the companies in China who still want access to Nvidia chips and the government who is saying, “No, no, no. Why don’t you try Chinese chips? Why don’t you help us with our Chinese domestic chip development?” There’s that divergence there. What’s interesting is players like Megaspeed in between could potentially do things like not just allow Chinese AI companies, again, to potentially get access to Nvidia chips, but then the argument some people are making is that those are chips that could have gone to the US AI companies and hyperscalers who are desperate. That is an argument that’s out there, but fundamentally, I don’t know how much of this is driven by those sheer commercial interests alone or, again, by some of these policy or ideological divides. Or by the influence of an alleged spy. Right, exactly. Because in a pure market environment, I think I know how this goes, but then you obviously have the complicated geopolitical dynamics and then you have this corruption element where both governments are attempting to influence one company at the center of the storm. What do you think happens if the Nvidia board investigation determines that Jensen acted inappropriately or a shareholder lawsuit imposes massive liability on Nvidia or a congressional investigation? There’s no way this company comes out of this unscathed, and the options are Jensen steps down or Nvidia’s restrained in some way or export controls go up even higher. Walk us through the probabilities and what you think happens next. There is a scenario actually where this ends up with not that much happening. Interesting. There is a pathway where there is a congressional investigation and they possibly find no wrongdoing or maybe Jensen really didn’t know, as he claims, that this Alice Huang person was a Chinese spy, and that this ends up feeding into the longer standing trajectory of all the export control debates and everything like that. That’s one possibility. Another possibility, though, is if there is some kind of wrongdoing that’s found, Jensen Huang might have to step down as CEO. He’s not just like a central node, he is like American AI, like the pillar that is holy. He’s the only one making the dollar. I mean, this is very important. Yeah, it’s like if you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that. I know that there’s a character he wants to play, where he’s in all the meetings and he’s probably taking some risk in chip design that is hard for us to see from the outside. But what we can see is Jensen’s enormous appetite for risk when it comes to financing neoclouds and investing in frontier AI companies. All of the dollars Nvidia is making flow back out in a circle to the AI ecosystem. It’s unclear to me whether that continues to happen without Jensen specifically being willing to front the risk and show up on CNBC as the face of the risk and say, “Everything’s okay.” What do you think happens then? His role as not just a technology leader, but as a market maker is really crucial. When he calls out certain companies like certain startups or neoclouds, you can see their stock prices go up. When he says something like, “I don’t know if this quantum thing is going to work out,” you saw the entire industry takes a hit. So that is the weight of his role in the broader ecosystem. Going forward, without that kind of advocate and this market maker playing this active role, that’s another factor. Beyond the Nvidia chips themselves and the technological role of the company, there is this deeper industry or even sociological function that Jensen plays and that Nvidia plays in this broader AI buildout. In some ways now, they’ve taken out someone who had otherwise for sheer commercial reasons been more aligned, and who’s going to take that place? If anything now, it has really charged the Democrats especially, who have been criticizing the Trump administration about not being tougher on these export controls. It has really galvanized the Democrats on this front and made it more of an issue perhaps than it was before. Yeah, especially when you connect it to corruption and the AI industry wasting money, all this stuff, it’s all there for them. Tell me more broadly about Chinese spying in the AI industry. There was a report, I don’t know, a few months ago that OpenAI was warning its employees that spies abound, that if suddenly attractive people appeared, be wary because they were probably spies. I love that. There’s just something about that that’s great. Obviously when it hits Jensen, it’s a different kind of story, especially with the national security implications and corruption implications. Give us a sense of what the spy trade is like on the ground for the average AI researcher. All I can say here is that they are juicy targets. For the US AI labs, anyone who’s involved with cutting-edge frontier AI, chip production, and chip design would be juicy targets for Chinese intelligence gathering because this is something where China’s trying to catch up. They’re trying to figure out how to keep pace with the US on AI and try to build their own alternatives to Nvidia GPUs. You can see there have been other examples of cases where they’ve been poaching engineers from TSMC in Taiwan or from South Korea, and have struggled to deal with efforts to hold back this strategic IP basically. There’s probably a lot more happening under the surface in terms of this cat-and-mouse game, but I do think that they are prime targets. Correct me if I’m wrong, but I think that there have been warnings from the US government to be careful and to step up your game on the cybersecurity front and the intelligence front to protect against these threats. Meanwhile, they’re putting all their information into Slack and getting breached on the daily. Who knows if these warnings are taking off. Whether it was above board or not — and there’s a rich debate you could have on that, we’ve had it on the show — they learned a lot from our companies. There was technology transfer. That’s happening in AI too. There are a lot of Chinese AI researchers working in and around these labs. There is technology transfer happening, again, above board or not. Isn’t that just the normal course of business or is there something more nefarious happening here? To some extent there are people flows and knowledge flows. You might not even think of it in terms of national-level AI communities. You might think about this global diffusion of know-how tips and tricks for squeezing a bit more performance out of the same amount of compute. Especially up until recently, you saw a lot of sharing of, say, papers like the transformer paper, that disseminated new architectural breakthroughs throughout the global AI community. Who gains and loses? I guess it’s also not just a one-way flow. Some of these American AI companies benefit a lot from having some of these Chinese developers work with them. In the same way Apple and Tesla, it wasn’t just like they gave away the crown jewels to China, but that China in turn saved these companies, especially at times when they were facing a perilous moment in their histories. There’s this bigger question about what the line is between normal commercial and technology flows versus a concerted state-backed effort to obtain sensitive strategic secrets and IP technology that would have broader geopolitical implications. Does that strategy for China look like a bunch of companies like Megaspeed with allegedly compromised executives, or does it play out more directly? Actually if anything, it would be less about the companies like Megaspeed, who seem to be middlemen for dealing with compute, and perhaps different companies, different agencies perhaps in the Chinese system, that might be more active. At one extreme you have the outright concerted efforts at industrial espionage. They’re state-backed actors who are very systematic at trying to obtain some of the best commercial secrets from around the world, including from American companies. But on the other hand, you do also have this gray zone of, “If a Chinese company acquires a stake in a US or European company, what does that mean? Does that mean they’re trying to obtain the technology or is that a regular commercial deal?” That’s where it starts to get more difficult to parse and you’d have to look at it on a case-by-case basis. One of the dynamics in talking about the Chinese government and the United States, especially when you talk to American industrialists, is that the American government is chaos and democracy is messy and everyone’s running in 50 different directions, and the Chinese system is directed. They make 100-year plans, not one-quarter plans. We’ve heard it. Everyone knows these cliches. How true is that? In this case alone, it doesn’t seem like they achieved the goal of their plan. In many cases, they might have actually set themselves back. Oh, yeah. For those who actually study China, who have done long-term research on this country and who understand it more closely, it looks like a much messier picture than any of these portrayals, especially from those in Silicon Valley who try to juxtapose China against what they find to be this annoyingly messy and unruly democracy. The Chinese system, both within the government and then across industries and government, is full of conflicting interests, rife with corruption. There are lots of times where you have bureaucratic turf wars that spill out into the open. You have missteps, ones that can backfire profoundly. You see that all the time. You see the local governments not following what Beijing wants, or following what Beijing wants but in the wrong direction. Sometimes they’re given a signal and they say, “Oh, okay, we got to run that way.” And then Beijing says, “No, no, no, no, no, other way, other way.” This happens all the time, and to anyone in Silicon Valley who’s trying to make this “neat” argument, all I can say is, go talk to people in China. They can tell you how messy it actually is on the ground. Kyle, this has been great. What do you think will happen next year? What should people be looking out for? The biggest thing is a congressional investigation and who’s behind that, what that surface is. And then potentially along with that, these pending bills around export controls and whether those will now get more momentum to pass in Congress, and whether Trump himself, and the White House in general, will try to play a role in either stopping that or giving that a quiet green light. I suspect we’re going to want to talk to you again as this process plays out. Thank you so much, Kyle, for being on Decoder. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. articles.title: Graph Label Alignment: A Diagnostic Atlas for Graph Classification
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14760v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph classification benchmarks vary widely in difficulty: some are solved by simple pooled baselines, while others remain challenging for GNNs and graph transformers. We take a data-centric view and ask whether benchmark success is driven by genuine structure--feature reasoning or by label signal already accessible from restricted marginal views. We introduce graph label alignment, a lightweight diagnostic that measures label accessibility through two supervised probes computed without training a graph encoder: structural label alignment (SLA), based on permutation-invariant topological and spectral summaries, and feature label alignment (FLA), based on pooled node features with edges removed. Across real graph classification benchmarks and multiple pooled backbones, the resulting SLA--FLA plane strongly organizes test accuracy, with low-alignment datasets forming a consistent regime where standard pooled pipelines struggle. To probe what lies beyond marginal accessibility, we introduce controlled interaction-dominated stress tests, including heterophilic ego-graphs and synthetic Twins tasks whose structural and feature marginals are matched across classes but whose role--feature couplings differ. These results show that high alignment explains much of easy benchmark performance, while low alignment reveals regimes where success requires preserving structure--feature correspondence beyond standard pooled representations.

articles.title: Distributionally Robust BEST-RQ For Speech Representation Learning
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.

articles.title: LLMs and the Homogenization of Teaching
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to lack diversity in open-ended text generation, a limitation that is especially consequential in education, where homogeneity can narrow the kinds of thinking and disciplinary work students are invited to do. We study diversity in two educational generation tasks: math items and essay feedback. We compare frontier and open-weight models with human-authored reference distributions using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures. For math, we examine the mathematical activities students are asked to perform; for feedback, we examine the revision work requested and the rhetorical strategies used to communicate it. We evaluate direct prompting, two diversity prompting methods, and post-training. Across both tasks, directly prompted model outputs are markedly less diverse than human-authored content--78% higher on lexical (Self-BLEU) and 51% higher on semantic (embedding) similarity--and represent a narrower range of instructional forms. Diversity prompting and post-training increase variation largely through surface features without broadening the instructional repertoire. Models inherit and amplify the most normative routines of human instruction. Overcoming mode collapse in education will require richer instructional data and investment in teachers' creative capacity and professional judgment.

articles.title: BirdDreams: Joint Perspective and BEV Video Generation for a Plausible, Reactive Driving World Model
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.

articles.title: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Sanskrit poses three challenges unresolved by single-call monolithic models: morphophonemic fusion Sandhi, dense nominal compounding Sam\=asa, and discourse-level zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel array of generalist gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers. Two separated judges evaluate quality: a routing judge ($J_{\text{route}}$, same model family as the generators) driving an internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge ($J_{\text{report}}=$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $85.90$ MQM against a monolithic baseline of $85.27$ ($\Delta=+0.63$, $p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018$, 95% CI $[+0.30,+0.97]$), and isolated discourse restoration alone accounts for $+0.44$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$), outperforming a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline by $+0.51$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$). articles.title: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14781v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $\theta$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_\theta$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_\theta$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_\theta$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_\theta$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.

articles.title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. articles.title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a model by up to 45 places.

articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Hy ASR 3.0, a large language model (LLM)-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) system that delivers strong recognition accuracy, supports flexible contextual conditioning, and maintains robust recognition performance across diverse speech conditions. Among the evaluated systems, it achieves the lowest aggregate error rates on public Mandarin Chinese, English, and Cantonese benchmarks and the lowest error rates on the corresponding internal test sets, alongside first-tier dialect recognition performance. Abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design.
